items.title: Harlem Labs: Survival and Ambition
items.content:
Harlem has always been more than a neighborhood; it is a living, breathing inheritance. From the electrifying heights of the Harlem Renaissance to the contemporary street corners that dictate global fashion and art, it remains a sanctuary where culture is forged, tested, and passed down. Drawing inspiration from the iconic narrative of The Wiz, a new visual project from Harlem Labs honors that deep legacy while charting an entirely original path forward for the modern creative.

At its heart, the project is a striking visual story about return, transformation, and the quiet courage required to be truly seen. Set against the vibrant, layered backdrop of Harlem, it follows a new generation of visionaries navigating the complex intersections of identity, survival, ambition, and community. Much like Dorothy’s journey down the yellow brick road, these artists eventually confront a universal truth: everything they have been searching for has existed within themselves, and within the community standing right beside them, all along.

The project is spearheaded by Harlem Labs, a multidisciplinary creative studio founded by Jamont Hanshaw that focuses on visual storytelling, creative direction, and collaborative artistry. For Hanshaw and the studio, this effort reflects the chaotic, beautiful reality of “creating while becoming.” It emphasizes the desperate need for spaces where emerging and historically underrepresented artists do not just survive, but feel profoundly supported, visible, and free to experiment without restraint.

Far transcending a standard fashion story, the work serves as a cultural manifesto. It poses a fundamental question: what happens when artists stop waiting for institutional permission and simply start building worlds of their own?

By rootedness in ancestral pride and an unwavering belief in self-determination, Harlem Labs isn’t just capturing culture—it is expanding the boundaries of what becomes possible when community becomes the canvas.

items.title: Gazing Through Chaos: Italo Calvino, seashells, and a conversation with Charles Negre
items.content:
Certain sensibilities are necessary not only for what they reveal about the era in which they belong, but because their influence extends far beyond their physical presence in the world. In this sense, Italo Calvino was a forerunner of something that is now glaringly obvious: we are increasingly unable to find points of reference within ourselves, a sense of balance, a verticality; we have forgotten the strategies to do so and have fewer and fewer resources to go back and seek them out.

Italo Calvino had a special relationship with the tangible world. Always divided, indecisive, a soul torn between two worlds: the real world and the other world—that is, the world of thought, of the words used to describe it. Italo Calvino, poor restless soul, was probably incapable of performing simple actions without thinking—leaving the house, taking a stroll, going to the sea, walking on the sand, watching the waves and the seagulls—he was unable to be satisfied with what he saw or heard. Within him burned the fire of something greater, like an impulse, a desire for a deeper connection with things.

In this sense, the sea was Calvino’s absolute destination of choice; the sea as an open theater, infinite by definition, a stage for his endless thoughts.

A young Italo Calvino wrote in a letter to Natalia Ginzburg that, having returned one day to his hometown of Sanremo to dispel the confusion of a reality he already found too touristy and teeming, and to regain his concentration, he began to draw, trying to copy some shells found in an old collection. The results were not masterpieces of the visual arts, but they were enough to quiet the chaos.

The practice, linked to close observation, to the meticulous search for details of form and color, linked to the hand, to the mark, to the tangible object, can become a way to create transparent walls around oneself, like a portable room where the goal is not to exclude oneself from reality, but to rediscover a center, to recalibrate, and then return to the outside world without succumbing to it.

The shell, in and of itself, is not a neutral entity: to use Calvino’s words, we might say that the shell is the singularity that contains multiplicity. A shell is a bridge between two universes, a primordial creature motionless yet alive, an ancient microcosm that lingers as a testament to what once was. In a tale from Cosmicomics, Italo Calvino has his protagonist—a creature that has travelled through the history of the universe—take the form of a mollusk, which, in an attempt to connect with its absolute aspiration for universal love, constructs its own shell, just as a sculptor builds his masterpiece. Through him, we discover that shells and the mollusks that inhabit them are blind creatures, and the marvel of their form is the result of their profound, intimate, and ancestral striving toward an unconditional desire for beauty—a desire that, however, can only acquire meaning through the eyes of those whom evolution has endowed with sight. It is, in other words, a gift they have provided for us.

Charles Negre is a French photographer, born in 1988 and working in Paris, whose practice spans between editorial and commercial photography as well as personal and artistic research. After graduating from the renowned ÉCAL, he has collaborated with leading contemporary fashion magazines and brands, in addition to personal projects with independent publishing houses. His work focuses primarily on studio photography and the still-life genre, which he continually reinterprets, moving in parallel with contemporary demands and the medium’s evolution, navigating the space between reality and construction. Furthermore, he explores the interplay between commissioned work and personal research, creating an extremely cohesive and consistent body of work. The Shells series engages with aesthetic elements characteristic of early still-life photography and plays with the ambiguity of familiar shapes; this retelling of a common object also encapsulates a fascination with the recurring patterns found in the symmetries inherent to natural elements.

Charles Negre’s shells are an exercise of the gaze, the final act of an exploration of form as a bridge between worlds. Through close observation and subsequent abstraction, the everyday transcends its own boundaries and appears in its most essential essence, as pure form, not as an empty vessel, but as a shifting structure. These forms are what remains beyond meaning, the unconditional beauty of which Calvino spoke.

This can only happen because, in Charles Negre’s images, objects hold absolute prominence; they appear, more than ever, in their material dimension, revealed through the attention devoted to roughness, which brings the sense of touch to the forefront. It is precisely the surfaces that serve as the space where their meaning is inscribed; the surface, in fact, is not to be understood as a mere container and physical appearance, but as a living space through which the outside and the inside can communicate—it’s the epidermis of things, vulnerable and sensitive. Calvino himself maintained that it is precisely through the surface of things that a profound knowledge of them becomes possible—or rather, that access to the infinity of meanings becomes possible.

So then, what is the relationship between Calvino’s drawings and the images we create today? When we talk about rediscovering a connection with things, what role do images play? Can we truly experience reality by observing it?

There is a knot that forms between the real, the tangible, and the gaze, and we are called upon to untangle it—or perhaps not to untangle it, but to recognize it. Perhaps, to truly “touch” things, we only need to rise above, pause, and look. Drawings, like photographs, and thus images in general, can serve as an exercise or a tool to grapple with the elusiveness of things and to escape the never-ending chaos of reality.

And while it is true that we must recognize the limits of our present, which carries us ever further away from material things and ever closer to their representations, at the same time we cannot resign ourselves to the idea that all is lost, because the tangible world is still here before us, doing nothing but reflecting us as we look at it. What we must do is learn to recognize it again.

Charles Negre: Still-life is actually all about that: stillness and slowing down the time to observe and document.

Marta Valdegrani: In the article, I compare your images from the Shells series with Italo Calvino’s drawings, and my conclusion is that maybe they are actually the same thing, in terms of process. To really touch reality, to be in contact with reality, it all comes through the gaze, through the act of looking; by making time to look at things in a different way.

C.N.: I think it’s about choosing to spend time to try to look at things with care. And once you take that time, then you start seeing things in mundane objects or random objects—some sort of spectacularity or specificity that makes objects look suddenly special. Shells are already spectacular, but in a way, everyone knows what a shell looks like. Only once you start looking closely can you begin to see a lot of elements in there. And I have the feeling that the pastas, in a way, are similar. One thing that is a bit funny is that they’re also artificial, they’re man-made, and they’re done by factories, but at the same time, this doesn’t take out some of the poetry that they carry, and their materiality. Our brain creates connections so that we have the feeling that the object is natural, but it’s not natural at all; we’re just looking at organic shapes and forms that kind of relate to our brain. So that’s quite a funny and interesting process.

M.V.: I also think that different things, even the most mundane things, have this sort of inner research for beauty, even though it doesn’t serve anything. Everything goes towards that ideal of beauty.

C.N.: There’s no hierarchy in beauty, in the sense that a beautiful piece of jewelry is just a beautiful piece of jewelry, and a beautiful piece of pasta by itself is something that could be looked at, and that can also be found beautiful. It’s just a matter of choosing what’s beautiful or not. And then with the help of photography, you can really translate it and use the light to highlight these natural connections that you see. It’s about using photography as a sort of witness to this thing.

M.V.: So if I interpret this correctly, maybe you would say there is no difference between a more mundane object and a more precious one?

C.N.: I think the concept of preciousness is really subjective; the things that someone could find precious are a result of their subjectivity. At work and at my place you could find many different objects, and one could be a really normal and uninteresting coffee cup, like a paper cup, but it could have a particular shape that is nice to look at or something written on it that is really funny, and it’s as important as something really nicely crafted. I think that it’s important to say that, depending on how you look at them, you can really find the beauty in these little objects.

M.V.: I think this is really evident mostly from your work that comes from commissions, but I can say for sure that it’s visible, maybe in a quieter way, also in your personal work. So, given that for you there is no hierarchy, I was wondering what your perception of the relationship between photography and reality is.

C.N.: Well, I think photography is a tool to look at reality. The photographer sees things and photography is a language to then show that to others. I use photography as a tool to witness nature and the world that surrounds us, and I only focus on objects and still objects because I feel they’re more honest, in a way. You see, objects can’t lie. In a way, it’s harder to find a way to photograph them than people. I take pictures of animals sometimes, but I think people are so complicated, because they come with a background; they come with a personality, and with so many things that you can have no other grip on. So, I feel like what comes out is not really honest. Whereas, if you shoot an apple, then an apple is an apple, and it’s the way you are going to photograph it that is going to make it special.

M.V.: And maybe with objects you, as the photographer, are able to become the subject of the picture in a more direct way.

C.N.: Of course, because once you start photographing objects, you are the mastermind behind the objects and you can create languages and conversations between them, which is a really important aspect and it’s also infinite; there are endless possibilities with it.

M.V.: So we could say that in the same way Calvino was drawing shells, maybe photography is your tool to find balance.

C.N.: Yes, I think so. Personally, I’ve never stopped making pictures. I’ve always photographed and I cannot stop doing it. It’s really complicated, I do it almost compulsively. Every time I find a new idea, maybe I don’t photograph it, but I keep the idea in my head, I draw it, I hold it there, because I know it could be a good photograph. I use photography as an everyday act, to just document the things I see, document the things I want to stage. To relate to what Calvino said, to me, photography is definitely a sort of therapy. Photography is really a way of looking at the world, and I think drawing is the same thing, the act of composing, making mental images. What I do is, I have a mental image that I want to try to recreate, and I let reality be involved in the process.

M.V.: Maybe a photograph doesn’t have inherent meaning, but the meaning comes through the effort that you make to capture reality.

C.N.: Exactly. And what’s really nice about photography, and maybe sometimes a bit frustrating with drawing, for example, is that with photography you have many parameters and tools you can use to build up your idea and your emotions. Composition, framing, light, it’s really highly technical, but all this technique helps you get to the idea you have in your mind. Some people get anxious in front of a white empty studio because it means having endless possibilities, but personally, I get excited because once I do one day of shooting in the studio, I know that I can spend another twenty years doing it and it always will be different because of those possibilities. I understand the stress of looking at an empty space, and I guess it’s the same thing with the white blank page for a writer, but there’s something so exciting about the idea of creating a world, of creating a conversation between objects that only lasts for a short period of time, and then it’s gone. I feel like people often think, for example with cinema, that emotions only come through character and people and life struggle and drama; but I think you can have a lot of drama through objects, a lot of emotions there. It’s just that as a photographer you have to be really subtle with your own emotions to be able to show that. For example, maybe that spider on your notebook could create a sort of strange emotion, or the image of a liquid in a bed could create a reminiscence. All these things can strike a chord in your brain.

M.V.: I think that your images offer a lot of room for interpretation, not in the sense that they force an interpretation, but they offer many ways in which they can make you feel. I have one last question and I don’t know if there’s an answer, really, but I know that shells are a recurring theme for you, because I read that, in addition to this series, you have a lot more pictures of actual shells in your archive. So I was wondering if, for you, there’s a memory or an emotion linked to this object.

C.N.: I think shells are highly symbolic. They have been a recurring image in history: the image of the shell was already present in early Dutch paintings. It’s the first thing you bring back from holidays as a kid, and one of the first things adventurers came back with, in the 16th century, from all over the world. But what I find mostly interesting is not really the real shell—I do have some real shells, and I do take photographs of them. But what I love most is calling a shell something that is not a shell. Let’s say that pasta is a shell; but the coffee cup that is left in a sewer or on the street is also a shell of some sort—a leftover. A shell is all the things that are a capsule of something else, and that you can’t use anymore. They’re just leftovers of recipients of something. All these things look like shells to me. I think shells also hold many layers of time. They’re like the circles inside trees, that once you cut them, you can go through time. They were also recipients of life, because every shell was an animal. The animal is now gone, and the shell is what is left. And maybe, also, a future recipient of something else.

items.title: Video of The Week: Why Do It?
items.content:
The film originated as David Fiene’s idea, born when he pointed a camera and asked a question that proved surprisingly difficult to answer properly throughout the entire shoot. Over the years, many explanations had been offered for why someone would choose to rise early to run, endure leg kicks that leave them unable to walk properly for days, or repeatedly return to a room where their shortcomings are laid bare, but most of those responses were merely convenient enough to end a conversation rather than reveal a fundamental truth.

Originally a secondary school mathematics teacher from New York who moved to Barcelona roughly nine years ago, she stumbled into Muay Thai almost by accident under the instruction of Pablo Rayo, having never considered herself an athlete nor searching for a sport. Like many women, she had survived sexual and domestic violence, responding by firmly deciding that anger was not the answer after seeing the destruction it could cause. Believing violence was never a solution, she kept her emotions hidden away and assumed she was fine, but Muay Thai stripped away that illusion not through mysticism, but through raw, visible struggle.

Being placed in situations where weakness, fatigue, and being out of one’s depth are exposed in front of others breaks through the surface, uncovering buried pain and leaving only the physical realization of whether one can fight back. Crucially, martial arts highlights the profound difference between pain inflicted without consent and pain that is willingly agreed to, where choosing the room, the partner, and the intensity allows the body to gradually relearn that it belongs to itself as the nervous system updates with new evidence. The genuine reason for continuing is not discipline, fitness, or enjoyment, but rather the reality that the pain is chosen, accompanied by a physical strength that contrasts sharply with past periods of powerlessness. This experience extends beyond any single individual or gender, speaking to anyone who has felt small or stripped of agency through illness, demanding work, grief, or immigration challenges, though women face an added societal expectation to take up less space and absorb impact rather than push back.

While hitting a pad for the first time often feels awkward or apologetic, consistent practice builds a presence that carries over into everyday life, prompting the co-founding of SOMA alongside Sevda Tunaboylu and Verena Walther to run free Muay Thai programs for migrant and refugee women in Barcelona. Clinical measurements consistently show meaningful improvements in wellbeing after every program cycle, yet the most convincing evidence remains watching participants realize they are allowed to stand their ground and be loud. Ultimately, the film offers no clean resolution to the central question, reflecting the reality that anyone claiming absolute certainty about enduring such repetitive discomfort is likely selling something, whereas the true significance lies simply in the ongoing act of choosing to step back into the room.

items.title: The Shifting Shapes of Self: Social Roles and Adaptability
items.content:
In modern society, identity is rarely a fixed or singular entity. Instead, we exist in a state of constant metamorphosis, continually reshaping ourselves to navigate the complex social roles we inhabit. We shift effortlessly—and sometimes painfully—between the professional, the familial, the vulnerable, and the rebellious. The Shifting Shapes of Self is a conceptual photographic series that captures this exact human fluidity, exploring how we adapt to the expectations of the environments around us.

Central to this visual exploration is Polina, who embodies four distinct archetypes within the series, each representing a different facet of the human experience. As the Saint Witch, she stands as a paradoxical figure blending the sacred and the forbidden, representing the tension between societal morality, innate wisdom, and hidden power.

In contrast, her portrayal of the Young Girl offers a portrait of innocence, raw vulnerability, and the unburdened curiosity that exists before the weight of external expectations takes hold. She then shifts into the Ambitious Prince, an embodiment of drive, authority, and rebellious agency that captures the hunger to conquer one’s circumstances and claim a place in the world. Finally, as the Person, she is stripped of all theatrical archetypes, grounding the series in raw, everyday humanity—the quiet, unmasked core that remains when all social performances fade away.

Through these contrasting personas, The Shifting Shapes of Self serves as both a mirror and a question. It asks where performance ends and authenticity begins, inviting viewers to reflect on the masks they wear, the roles they play, and the true nature of the self hidden beneath them all.

items.title: Im Halbschatten: Echoes of a Forgotten Dress
items.content:
By engaging with the history of the Jewish fashion industry in Germany and its systematic, forced Aryanization during National Socialism, the project examines what remains hidden or forgotten, yet continues to be passed down subconsciously through generations.

Tracing back the origins of the designer’s great-grandmother’s dress, the work highlights how she had sewn it for herself to attend her younger sister’s wedding in 1944. Gertraud and Walther—the designer’s great-grandparents—were prohibited from marrying, even though engaged, because Walther was half-Jewish.

The original dress carries the physical traces of these political transformations, visible in its pattern, fabric, and construction. Through careful analysis and deconstruction, new garments emerged from this history. Moritz and Daria—who is Jewish herself—become the physical vessels through which the complex gender dynamics between Walther and Gertraud are reconsidered. Materially, thick wool layers conceal delicate silk underneath; one has to literally move through these heavy layers to uncover the shadows passed down through generations, lingering beneath the skin. Through motion, unexpected openings reveal the hidden, delicate fabrics and intricate embroidery beneath.

Daria’s trousers, worn in the photographs by Ludwig, open through embroidered pockets that directly reference the domestic textile work idealized onto women, contrasting sharply with rigid military pattern construction. All three trousers in the collection feature an extra-deep crotch, prioritizing comfort, free movement, and an exploration of androgyny. Constructed from a mixture of deadstock fabrics, leftovers, and antique flea market finds, the collection balances historical gravity with contemporary utility. Despite their historical weight, these clothes are meant to be lived in—to move, to play, and possibly even to play football in. Captured on a Sunday afternoon at Humboldthain in Berlin by photographer Ida Weber, the accompanying imagery utilizes two analogue formats to catch the models in fluid motion, blending the ghosts of the past with the vitality of the present.

items.title: Things Learned and Unlearned: A Conversation with 25KG’s Konstantin Grcic
items.content:
Ontologically, the “thing” is an elusive category—so broad and expansive that it seems to belong more to the realm of ideas than to that of material reality. Yet we live in a culture obsessed with naming, classifying, and pigeonholing every object into a specific function, stabilising its charge and disarming its potential. With 25KG, his latest project, Konstantin Grcic turns the ontological condition of things into the very engine of radicality. Not as an assault on the status quo, as it used to be, but as the introduction of generative doubt: a condition of ambiguity, ambivalence, and multivalence in which objects are meant to be experienced, handled, and lived through unexpected interactions and constantly shifting readings. More than a collection of furniture, 25KG questions the very notion of furnishing itself, opening up new possibilities for how we relate to the things around us. In these pages, Grcic discusses the project and its intersections with both the contemporary design landscape and the traditions that continue to shape it.

Daria Miricola: 25KG is a rather loaded name: it folds together the founding year, 2025, and your initials, but it also reads as a literal unit of weight. Where did the idea originate, and what kind of gravity did you want the label to carry from the outset?

Konstantin Grcic: Ever since I was a child, I knew my initials were the same as ‘kilogram.’ I always liked that—and also the pictogram of the cast-iron weight. So the idea had been with me for a very long time. 25KG was the right moment to use it. Why 25? I needed a name that could be registered as a trademark. And, incidentally, 25 kg is a weight most people can lift—which is why disaster-relief sandbags weigh 25 kg.

DM: The radical design movements of the ‘60s and ’70s operated in open antagonism toward bourgeois domesticity and consumer culture. Do you think the cultural meaning of furniture has shifted since then? In other words: does a radical object still have the same capacity to destabilise the status quo, or has design itself become too self-aware for that?

KG: Yes, I think the meaning of furniture has changed. In the ‘60s and ’70s, radical design still believed objects could directly challenge society. Today, design is much more self-aware—and quickly absorbed by the market, media and culture industry. Even radical gestures become style very fast. But objects can still unsettle us in quieter ways: through ambiguity, discomfort, humour, vulnerability, or by resisting easy categorisation. Perhaps radicality today is less about opposition and more about creating doubt, friction or emotional complexity within everyday life.

DM: More broadly, what is the condition of the European design scene today? Where do you sense genuine vitality, and where do you feel the ﬁeld has become complacent or risk-averse?

KG: There is still a great deal of vitality in the European design scene—especially in smaller, independent structures where design, research, craft and culture overlap more freely. I often find the most interesting work happening at the edges, outside the large commercial system.

At the same time, much of mainstream design has become cautious and overly image-conscious. There is a strong tendency toward safe aesthetics, familiar narratives, and market-friendly ideas. Risk today is often simulated, rather than truly taken.

DM: You have worked for decades within large industrial ecosystems while simultaneously maintaining a highly singular authorial voice. How different is it to operate through your own platform, 25KG, rather than through established clients and manufacturers? What do you gain—and lose—in each model?

KG: Working through my own platform, 25KG, gives me a different kind of freedom and immediacy. Decisions become faster, more instinctive, and sometimes more personal. At the same time, it also means taking responsibility for everything—production, logistics, communication… and risk.

Working with established manufacturers is slower and more complex, but it allows projects to develop with greater industrial depth, technical precision and long-term impact. Ideally, both models nourish each other.

DM: 25KG presents objects simply as ‘THINGS,’ catalogued according to the order in which they appear: THING_01, THING_02, and so on. There is something almost proto-scientiﬁc, or even deadpan, about that protocol.Where does this taxonomy come from?

KG: The taxonomy is intentionally neutral and open. I liked the idea of avoiding predefined categories or narratives and simply letting things appear one after another, almost like findings or observations. The term THING felt direct, unpretentious, and slightly anonymous—which gives the objects more freedom to become whatever people imagine them to be.

DM: The ﬁrst THINGS already seem to share a trajectory or common grammar: raw materials, structural directness, an almost anti-rhetorical clarity. Are you consciously building a language, or do you prefer to let afﬁnities emerge a posteriori?

KG: I’m not trying to build a “language” in a strategic sense. For me, it’s more about attitude. I think there’s a major shortcoming in the industry in this regard. Attitude is something very valuable… but of course it also demands a lot. Strength, confidence, perseverance. The affinities emerge quite naturally through the way we work and what interests us—structure, directness, reduction, certain materials, certain moods. Over time, connections become visible almost by themselves.

DM: How does 25KG approach pricing and communication without falling back on the usual luxury design tropes?

KG: By trying to stay direct and transparent. We avoid artificial narratives of exclusivity and instead focus on the objects themselves—how they are made, used, and communicated. The challenge is to remain accessible without becoming generic, and precise without becoming corporate.

DM: Your work has often generated sharply polarised reactions. Chair_ONE, for instance, is now cult, yet when it ﬁrst appeared it triggered fascination, bewilderment, even ridicule in certain circles. How do you personally relate to the idea of controversy?

I never saw controversy as a goal in itself. Usually, it simply means that something unsettles existing expectations. If a project creates strong reactions, positive or negative, it often means it touched a nerve. Over time, people tend to become more comfortable with things that initially felt strange, and that grows a stronger bond.

DM: And once a controversial object becomes institutionalised—collected by museums, canonised by the market—does it lose part of its original charge? What does it take today for a piece of furniture to still feel genuinely controversial?

KG: Yes, inevitably, once an object becomes familiar, collected, and historically absorbed, part of its disruptive energy disappears. Today, genuinely controversial furniture is probably less about shocking form and more about questioning systems of production, value, use, or desire in subtle and intelligent ways.

DM: Finally, which future THINGS are currently taking shape? And more importantly: are there territories—materially, politically, or culturally—that you still feel design has not fully managed to tap into?

KG: There are several new THINGS taking shape at the moment. What still interests me are territories where design becomes less resolved and more open. I think design still struggles with ambiguity. It often wants to explain too much, optimise too much, behave too correctly.

items.title: Kolios: emptiness and Negative Space
items.content:
KOILOS—derived from the ancient Greek word κοῖλος, meaning hollow, concave, or cavity—serves as the foundational concept for a fashion story photographed by Marcello Ferri and styled and art-directed by Mariia Khrebtova. Rooted in a minimal visual language, the project pivots away from loud, performative expressions of femininity, choosing instead to explore softness, silence, and sculptural form as a nuanced visual and emotional language.

The narrative treats the female form not as a mere figure, but as an architectural presence that interacts intimately with light, fabric, and surrounding space. Emptiness and negative space are given primary agency; the body functions almost like a sculpted object inhabiting an environment, creating a subtle yet palpable tension between presence and absence, fragility and structure.

Drawing heavily from an architectural sensibility, the story operates on the principle that void and silence themselves have the power to define atmosphere, shape raw emotion, and mold physical form into an introspective celebration of quiet femininity.

items.title: Furore Grand Hotel: The Horizon Has No Edge
items.content:
There is a moment on the road to Furore when the Amalfi Coast ceases to resemble geography and begins to feel like vertigo. The road coils above the Tyrrhenian Sea, villages appear improbably fastened to cliffs, and the water below seems less like something one might swim in than a vast blue atmosphere. By the time I arrived at Furore Grand Hotel, I had the peculiar sensation of having gained altitude without ever leaving the ground.

The view explains it. From the hotel’s terraces, the Mediterranean spreads out with almost no foreground to contain it. You do not look toward the sea so much as hover above it, as though seeing the coastline from a helicopter. Praiano rests in the distance; farther out, the horizon becomes a fine seam between two shades of blue. At certain hours even that seam disappears.

Furore is often called the village that does not exist, because its houses are scattered across the mountainside rather than gathered around a recognizable center. The hotel, opened in 2023 after a four-year renovation, seems to embrace that elusive quality. Set across nine green terraces between Amalfi and Positano, it appears less constructed upon the landscape than suspended within it.

Its two pools deepen the illusion. The main infinity pool runs along the white façade, with loungers partially immersed in the shallow water. Below, a quieter pool forms part of the spa’s outdoor circuit. From either, the edges seem to dissolve into the sea until pool, ocean and sky become an infinite extension of blues. Swimming there can feel disorienting in the loveliest way: the body remains close to the hotel while the eye travels miles from shore.

White is the hotel’s governing language. Walls, arches, terraces and vaulted interiors have been stripped of visual noise, allowing daylight and the colors outside to enter freely. The effect is not austere. It is closer to being aboard a serene Mediterranean spaceship—one furnished with hand-painted ceramics from Vietri sul Mare, softly curved furniture and an exquisite collection of glassware displayed throughout the property. Each vessel catches the light differently, holding little fragments of sea and sunset.

My room, one of the hotel’s Signature Pool Suites, opened onto a private garden where an olive tree leaned over a plunge pool. Jasmine and Mediterranean plants softened the immaculate geometry. I could swim beneath the tree at night, when the water reflected the darkness, and again in the morning as the first light reached the terrace. Sunrise and sunset were not events to be watched through a window; they entered the room’s daily rhythm. Luxury here was not announced by a single extravagant gesture. It accumulated quietly in the garden, the glassware, the crisp whites, the precise placement of a chair facing the horizon—until it seemed to spring from everywhere.

Beyond the suites, paths descend through gardens planted with herbs, flowers, olive trees and coastal vegetation. The landscaping recalls the Amalfi Coast’s agricultural terraces while resisting their rustic clichés. Everything feels meticulous, but never sealed off from nature. Rosemary scents the air. Bougainvillea supplies flashes of magenta against the white. The sea remains visible between branches.

Breakfast was perhaps the hotel at its most intimate. At Velaris, beneath white sails overlooking the coast, the morning unfolded slowly: pastries presented at the table, eggs made to order, fresh juices and infusions, and espresso scented with lemon peel, prepared in a Neapolitan cuccumella. It was one of the warmest breakfasts I have experienced in a hotel—and I have spent a considerable part of my life in hotels. Its comfort came not only from the food but from the people serving it, who understood that genuine hospitality is a matter of attention rather than ceremony.

That same attentiveness shaped the days. The staff composed our itinerary with the fluency of editors, arranging the coast into a sequence that felt personal rather than programmed. At Bluh Furore, the hotel’s Michelin-starred restaurant, Executive Chef Vincenzo Russo’s meal offered another kind of itinerary: a progression through Campania, interpreted with precision but grounded in recognizable flavors. Local wines, many from small producers working on the region’s steep terrain, gave the dinner a sense of place that no panoramic view alone could accomplish.

And yet the view remained the hotel’s most persuasive luxury. In a region where beauty is abundant enough to become almost theatrical, Furore Grand Hotel has found a way to frame it without overpowering it. Late in the day, the white terraces took on the peach and lavender tones of the sky. The pools darkened, then briefly caught the last light. From beneath the olive tree, I watched the boundaries disappear again—the garden into the room, the pool into the sea, the sea into the sky—and understood that the hotel’s great achievement was not bringing the outdoors inside. It was making inside and outside feel like distinctions that no longer mattered.

items.title: South of Florida: The Boys of Eternal June
items.content:
You know the type before you know his name: two big fish in each hand, a well-earned look of pride, sun-kissed skin, golden hair, a boat idling at the dock, and a beautiful girlfriend. The type of boy who reliably appears along the South Florida coast. In certain places, it’s always June. It’s always summertime. They have a way of producing boys like this: sun-bleached not by styling but by lifestyle, shaped by open windows and longer summers.

To understand this archetype, you have to understand the geography that breeds it. On the barrier islands and intracoastal stretches running from Jupiter down through Islamorada, life is calculated not in months or quarters, but in tides and weather windows. The calendar may technically say November, but the air still carries the humid weight of early afternoon rain, and the water stays warmer than most hotel pools. In places where winter is just a brief couple of weeks in late January when the temperature drops into the fifties, season-switching never happens.

Clothes don’t get rotated out; they just get worn until the saltwater and sun break them down. The golden hair isn’t from a salon on Worth Avenue; it’s the inevitable chemical result of twelve hours a day spent under an unfiltered subtropical sun, mixed with ocean spray that dries into fine salt crystals on the skin. For these boys, the boat isn’t a weekend luxury or a status symbol flexed for social media. It’s an extension of the driveway—a primary mode of existing.

There is a specific kind of confidence that comes from growing up entirely outdoors. It isn’t loud or performative. It’s built on practical competence that looks seamless to outsiders: knowing the exact depth of a sandbar by the slight shift in blue-green hue, docking a twin-engine center console in a stiff crosswind without raising a voice, and living by a natural rhythm dictated by when the mahi are running offshore or when the tide turns at the inlet.

items.title: Il Monastero: Ischia’s Grand Œuvre
items.content:
The first glimpse arrives before the island does. From the ferry, as Ischia draws nearer in the afternoon, the Castello Aragonese appears to rise directly from the Mediterranean: a mass of stone crowned by pale buildings, suspended between the blue of the water and the blue of the sky. At that hour, the sun falls across its walls with the improbable softness of cinema. The fortress seems less constructed than conjured, waiting offshore like a mirage.

Only after disembarking does its geography become clear. The Castello occupies its own trachytic-rock islet, separated from Ischia by a narrow strip of sea and joined to it by a 230-meter-long masonry bridge. To reach Il Monastero, the hotel hidden near its summit, one must cross the bridge in its entirety, enter the base of the rock and step into an elevator that ascends through a tunnel carved into the mountain. The journey takes barely a minute, yet it feels like a passage between worlds.

Emerging at the top, I was met by a panorama so expansive that, for a moment, the hotel itself seemed secondary. Ischia unfolded below in a succession of tiled roofs, green hills and crescent-shaped coves. Beyond it were Procida and Vivara, and farther still the hazy outline of the Campanian coast. The Mediterranean stretched outward until distance dissolved its edges. It was easy to feel caught inside the sun-dazed world of The Talented Mr. Ripley, which found part of its Italy here. Il Monastero occupies a former convent founded in 1575 for cloistered Clarisse nuns. Its 19 rooms and two suites retain something of their original cells: whitewashed walls, vaulted ceilings and a deliberate scarcity of furniture. Wrought-iron beds, locally made pieces and blue majolica floors provide the decoration. Yet austerity here does not feel like deprivation. The absence of excess directs one’s attention toward other things—the movement of light, the cries of gulls, the texture of old plaster and the sea framed by a window.

The hotel grew from an appropriately spare form of hospitality. Beginning in the 1970s, travelers wishing to sleep in the abandoned convent were given sheets and candles for the night—and, in the earliest days, a bucket of water. It was a romantic, if rudimentary, arrangement that became the foundation for what was then called L’Albergo del Monastero. The construction of the elevator through the volcanic rock made hospitality, and the transportation of life’s necessities, considerably easier.

The Castello itself had been purchased from the Italian state in 1912 by the lawyer Nicola Ernesto Mattera: 25,000 lire for what amounted to 25 centuries of neglected history. Its fortress, prisons, churches, gardens and convent stood largely in ruins. Today, the third generation of the Mattera family continues the work of restoring it—not as a relic sealed off from life, but as an inhabited cultural landscape.

Over breakfast, I met Anna Cristina Mattera, whose parents, the painter Gabriele Mattera and the German graphic designer Karin Mattera, helped revive the Castello beginning in the 1970s. Cristina spoke of their life among its ruins and of the artists who gathered there. Her father’s paintings now hang throughout the hotel, not as decorative afterthoughts but as extensions of the architecture. Their colors appear to have been chosen in conversation with the chalky walls, volcanic earth and mutable blues of the sea.

Art is everywhere, though rarely announced. Works by family friends and artists who have passed through the Castello occupy corridors and dining rooms. The former refectory of the nuns, later Gabriele’s studio, has become loStudio, a shop devoted to carefully selected Italian art and craft. Outside, the old hortus conclusus has been transformed into a luminous garden of vines, vegetables and native plants. In the afternoon, its leaves seem to hold the sunlight.

Meals are served on a terrace where the view renders conversation momentarily unnecessary. At breakfast, lunch and dinner, Ischia appears in a different register: pearly in the morning, sharply colored at noon, then gradually softened by dusk. From this height, the island looks both near enough to touch and impossibly remote. The effect is not unlike dining on another planet—one with excellent pasta and a sea breeze.

The following day, from a boat circling the Castello, I saw the rock from below. We swam beneath its walls, where volcanic bubbles rose through the water and broke silently at the surface. Above us were centuries of fortification, faith, abandonment and repair; below, the island remained geologically alive.

Many hotels attempt to manufacture a sense of escape. Il Monastero offers something stranger and more affecting: the privilege of briefly entering a place shaped by time rather than designed against it. Its beauty is not immaculate. It lies in the accumulated intention—in every repaired vault, planted terrace, inherited painting and wall left bearing the evidence of age. The Matteras have spent generations making a masterpiece, though perhaps their greatest achievement has been knowing where not to interfere. Here, light remains the principal architect, the sea the dominant artwork and silence the rarest luxury of all.

items.title: Passing Through: Choreography of Urban Solitude
items.content:
Two women move through the same city, navigating an identical geography of transit. They descend into the same fluorescent-lit metro stations, cross the same concrete underpasses, and wait on the same railway platforms. Their paths intersect on paper and align in space, yet their trajectories remain strictly parallel. They never meet.

This photographic project investigates the hidden geometry of contemporary urban existence. Cities are often defined by their density and friction, yet the spaces of transit—the non-places of departure and arrival—frequently produce a distinct form of isolation. Side by side, countless individual lives unfold in perfect synchrony, bound by shared routes but separated by the invisible boundaries of strangerhood. The city functions as an unwitting stage, hosting a quiet choreography of proximity without connection.

Shot on color negative film and hand-printed in the darkroom via optical enlargement, the work deliberate grounds itself in the physical medium of photography. In an era dominated by hyper-visible digital immediacy, the analogue process introduces a tangible weight to these transient moments. Grain, color depth, and the physical exposure of light onto paper reflect the themes at the heart of the project: presence, absence, fleeting coincidences, and the fragile, unfulfilled potential for human encounter.

These photographs do not seek out extraordinary events; instead, they observe the suspended moments in between. Paused between where they have been and where they are going, the subjects inhabit a subtle tension between emotional intimacy and physical distance—a quiet reflection of how we inhabit the modern city together, yet alone.

items.title: Video Of The Week: Flights
items.content:
In her celebrated novel Flights, Olga Tokarczuk presents a world in perpetual transit—a constellation of narratives, fragments, and essays where movement is not merely a means of travel, but a philosophical condition. Drawing deep thematic inspiration from Tokarczuk’s mosaic-like structure, a compelling new cinematic work emerges to tackle the fundamental tension between motion and stillness, vitality and slow decay. Rather than relying on a traditional, linear plot, the film constructs a fluid architecture of three interwoven narratives, offering a meditation on human existence continuously negotiated between opposing destinations.

The film’s power lies in its contrasting character studies, each embodying a different aspect of this spatial and psychological conflict. The first narrative centers on a figure consumed by ritual and accumulation, trapped in an internal paralysis that turns domestic life into a static tableau. In stark contrast, the second thread follows a restless body moving endlessly through the modern city—a modern nomad whose constant physical displacement reflects a refusal to settle into an established identity. Unifying these opposing worlds is a third, enigmatic presence: a figure who functions less as a traditional character and more as a manifestation of raw emotional force, subtly altering the atmospheric energy and psychological gravity of every room he enters.

Visually and rhythmically, the film mirror-images its thematic dualities. Prolonged, static tableaux are set against drifting, wandering camera movements, creating a hypnotic cadence that echoes Tokarczuk’s prose. These juxtaposed passages suggest that personal identity, much like narrative cinema itself, is never permanent. Instead, it is a fragile state shaped by the dialectic between staying and fleeing, living and decomposing.

items.title: ‘Corpo a Corpo’: In Conversation With Chiara Enzo
items.content:
For Chiara Enzo, touching and painting are not, after all, such different things. Born in 1989, the Venetian artist creates intimate images, often small in scale, that invite the viewer to look at them closely, almost to brush against them. Fragments of the world that never exceed the size of a human face and that have the power to make us almost touch (and imagine) a landscape made up of skin, bodies and layered textures.

At a time when we experience the world primarily through screens, touch seems to have become a secondary sense. Yet the desire to touch—others, images, objects—continues to exist, even when it manifests itself merely as a tension in the gaze. For Enzo, painting arises exactly from this tension: from a constant ‘hand-to-hand’ engagement with images, with the surface, and with reality itself.

Alessia Baranello: I’d like to start with the theme of this issue: the need to touch others and the world in order to understand them better. Is there anything that, in your view, we no longer touch enough these days?

Chiara Enzo: I think we’re forgetting about touch as a means of understanding. Today, our relationship with the world is primarily mediated by immediate vision: the interface we use most is video, the screen. And there, the dimension of physical contact disappears almost entirely.

It’s curious because we continue to use touch all the time, but in a different way: we touch screens, zoom in on images, and get closer to things through our phones rather than with our bodies. With those closest to us, physical contact remains. What we are losing, however, is touch as a way of exploring the world.

 

AB: In your own experience, when you want to get to know something—a person, an image, a subject to paint—what is the first thing you do to feel a connection?

CE: It’s not really about touching, also because I’m a rather shy person. But I’ve always used my gaze in an almost tactile way. When I’m faced with a subject that interests me, the first thing I do is observe it very closely. At some point, there’s always something—a shape, a situation—that has an impact on me. Even before I understand why that thing interests me, I acknowledge the fact that it has struck me.

It might be attraction, it might be repulsion, but in any case there’s an impact. And so I start observing and drawing, because for me drawing is an extension of observation. Often it’s only in the aftermath that I really manage to understand what happened in that exchange.

What is represented in the final image is not so much the object itself, but rather the record of the interaction that took place with that object or with that presence. Ultimately, much of my work is precisely about this: not so much the things themselves, but the relationship I have with things and with the world.

 

AB: Do you remember the first thing you ever drew?

CE: The first drawing I can consciously remember is a mountain landscape, probably the Dolomites. As a child, I spent every summer there with my family, and for me it was a place of total discovery, completely different from everyday life.

I drew a great lot. I think drawing was my first real tool for understanding the world, even before I realised it. It has always been the way I’ve clung to reality.

AB: Your work often focuses on the body and its fragments. What is your relationship with other people’s bodies?

CE: My work simply reflects the way I see the world. The fact that my images often feature very close-up shots corresponds to how I mentally register things. When I meet someone, I never perceive them in a completely holistic way: my mind breaks them down, fragments them, constructs a sort of map. At that point, a person becomes almost like a landscape.

AB: When you paint in detail, do you ever feel as if you can touch what you’re depicting?

CE: It’s more complicated than that. For me, the tactility of the gaze is the embodiment of a desire. But it’s a desire that never truly comes to fruition. And that’s precisely why it remains alive and transforms into energy. In the images I choose, you can sense this physical intention of the gaze: it translates into the framing, the shift in focus, the internal tension.

My works are often asymmetrical; they have their own silent dynamics. What I want to capture is precisely this desire of the gaze to become tactile. Real contact never fully occurs, but it is precisely the impossibility of contact that produces the energy that interests me.

AB: Do you think that those who view your work feel this same desire for connection?

CE: It’s very subjective. No image speaks to everyone in the same way. What interests me, however, is seeking out images that can be recognised as shared human experiences. I always start from my own personal experience, but I constantly ask myself whether that feeling might also resonate with others.

My desire has always been for connection, even if mediated by the image. For me, my work is a bridge to others. When this connection is made, then it means the work is working.

AB: Do you feel that painting has also been a way for you to overcome a certain shyness?

CE: Shyness certainly played a part, particularly in my choice of a form of expression that didn’t place me directly in the spotlight. In painting, the work becomes something separate from the person who created it.

AB: There is also a very physical aspect to your working process. What is your relationship with the artistic medium?

CE: When I work, a kind of alignment occurs between what I see and the surface of the image. That desire for contact I mentioned earlier is fully transferred into the work through a very physical process, and the image becomes the catalyst for all that energy, almost the victim of that intensity. I focus intensely on the surface, almost to the point of disfiguring it. I work on small formats, using very hard, sharp pencils that scratch the paper. I fill tiny surfaces with a densely woven pattern of marks, almost as if it were fabric.

The resulting works are always poised between fragility and destruction, between delicacy and a form of hidden aggression. This is another reason why I feel it is difficult to truly explain my work through a photograph. Only by looking at the work in person does one realise this ‘hand-to-hand struggle’ I have had with the surface.

AB: These days, painting is often seen as something detached from reality, almost as if it were the most abstract of contemporary artistic languages. For you, however, the opposite seems to be true.

CE: For me, the act of painting is essential for staying grounded in reality. Using your hands, touching—that’s what it means.

Painting is simultaneously the most primitive medium possible, and one of the most complex. Making a mark in the sand is already painting: it is a primal gesture. But at the same time, painting carries with it a history stretching back thousands of years which cannot be ignored.

What I find in painting—and what I struggle most to find in other media—is above all the obligation to take one’s time. The act of painting consists first and foremost of observation: ninety per cent of the work is simply looking.

And looking, for me, means staying grounded in reality, keeping one’s feet on the ground.

items.title: HACOY: Denim Collection
items.content:
In an industry dominated by rapid cycles and fleeting trends, a quiet revolution is taking shape through thoughtful craftsmanship and deliberate patience. This interview dives into the philosophy behind a new unisex denim collection designed to endure, starting with the conscious selection of an honest, mid-weight organic cotton and hemp blend. Stepping entirely off the traditional seasonal fashion calendar, the designer behind this vision discusses the advantages of a localized preorder production model, the balance between a subtle design signature and timeless versatility, and how nostalgic memories of carefree student life translate into relaxed, everyday cuts. What emerges is a blueprint for the future of conscious design—where beauty, durability, and responsibility coexist seamlessly, proving that the most impactful garments are those built to be lived in for years, not just a season.

The collection uses a specific two-thirds organic cotton and one-third hemp blend. Can you take us through the development of this fabric?

We did not engineer this fabric ourselves, we found it. It comes from a partner mill, and choosing it was its own kind of work. Most denim that looks beautiful is either heavy and stiff, or it feels soft only because it has been treated and washed to death. I was looking for something honest, hardwearing, that still breathed. This organic cotton and hemp cloth was the one that did all three. The hemp gives it structure and longevity, the cotton keeps it soft against the skin, and organic on both sides keeps the impact low. At roughly two thirds cotton and one third hemp, around a mid weight of 315 grams, it holds its shape, ages well, and still moves with you. Our job was not to invent the textile, it was to recognise the right one and build the pieces around it.

 

Why do you think more brands haven’t adopted hemp, and how does HACOY hope to change that perception?

Honestly, because hemp is harder to work with and slower to source at scale, and most of the industry is built for speed and volume. It needs the right mill, the right blend, the right finishing, and none of that fits a calendar that wants a new drop every few weeks. There is also an old image problem, people still associate hemp with something rough or crunchy, a sack rather than a garment. We want to quietly break that association by simply making a piece that feels good and looks like proper denim, and letting people discover the fibre underneath. If the jeans feel right on the body, the sustainability stops being a lecture and becomes something you can feel.

How do you educate your customers to embrace the wait, and how does the preorder model impact your production timeline in Italy?

We do not really try to sell the wait, we explain how it works, and people respond well to honesty. The model is simple. We open preorders and wait until we reach a minimum number, because that is the point where production makes sense and nothing has to be made speculatively. Once we hit that number, we check the timing with our production partner so we can give everyone a realistic window. Customers pay fifty percent upfront, and only then do we kick off the manufacturing in Italy. The other half follows closer to delivery. What holds it all together is transparent communication on both sides, our customers know exactly when and what is happening, and so does the workshop. Nobody is left guessing, and nothing is made that someone has not already chosen. The waiting becomes part of owning the piece, you anticipate it, and when it arrives it means more.

How does stepping off the traditional fashion calendar change the way you approach design, and how does it support the financial sustainability of a growing brand?

Stepping off the seasonal calendar frees you to design the right piece instead of the next piece. We are not chasing four collections a year, so we can spend the time to get one garment properly right and then keep it. Everything we make is meant to stay in the range and stay in your wardrobe, so we design for years, not for a window. And because we never discount, the price you see is simply the honest price, we are not inflating it in spring to cut it in autumn. That is actually healthier for a growing brand, we hold our margin, we hold our value, and we build slowly on pieces that keep selling rather than on a spike that has to be cleared out three months later.

 

How do those memories of “carefree lightness” translate into the physical cuts and silhouettes of the jeans and jacket?

The collection grew out of my own student time at Polimoda in Italy, and the feeling I carried away from it. There is a certain Italian lightness to being a student there, sitting outside with friends, no rush, living in the moment before everyone was permanently online. I always think of the spirit of 1980s Italian student life, a time before social media, that same carefree ease. In the garments that becomes a relaxed cut rather than a tight one, room to move, nothing that pinches or performs. The jacket is easy over the shoulders, the jeans sit comfortably and age with you. It is denim you throw on to meet people, not denim you have to think about. That lightness is the memory, and the cut is how you wear it.

How do you balance creating a distinct brand “signature” while keeping the garments truly timeless and versatile for a unisex audience?

The rule we set ourselves is that the signature should reward a second look, never demand the first one. The two tone panels give the piece its own quiet identity, you can tell it apart across a room, but it reads as denim, not as a logo statement. The monogram is deliberately discreet, it is there for the person wearing it more than for everyone watching. We keep the silhouette unisex and clean so the same piece works on very different bodies and very different lives. A signature that shouts dates quickly, a signature that whispers can stay timeless. We would rather someone wear these jeans for ten years than recognise them for one season.

How do you select your production partners, and how do you ensure your ethical and quality standards are met across borders?

We choose partners the slow way, by talking, testing, and building relationships over time rather than shopping around for the cheapest option. We found this fabric through Fabricsight, a partner we have worked with for over a year now on fabric scouting and sourcing, and who we trust to bring us the right cloth. The denim itself is woven in Turkey, and the garments are cut and sewn in Italy where the craft and the finishing are exceptional. We also work with trusted workshops in Lithuania on other lines. What ties it together is that these are real relationships, not anonymous suppliers, we know the people we work with and we keep the circle small enough to actually oversee. Standards hold when you stay close, so we would rather work with a few partners we trust deeply than spread across many we never see.

 

As a member of the New European Bauhaus, how does that membership influence HACOY’s long-term vision? What can we expect next after denim?

The New European Bauhaus says something we already believed, that sustainability and beauty are not a trade off, they belong together. A responsible piece still has to be something you really want to wear, otherwise the sustainability is meaningless. That membership keeps us honest about designing for the long term, for durability, for pieces that earn their place rather than pieces that impress once. After denim we keep building the same wardrobe outward, our home office clothing, our essentials, always the same idea of comfort and lightness made responsibly. We are not in a hurry to be everywhere. We would rather add one considered piece at a time and let the brand grow the way the clothes are meant to be worn, slowly and for years.

items.title: Designing the Temporary to Be Timeless: Inside Studio Musa’s Domestic Universe for 545
items.content:
There is a distinct friction at the heart of contemporary design—a constant, quiet tug-of-war between the fleeting velocity of fashion and the grounded permanence of architecture. We live in an era of the ephemeral, where spaces are built for a weekend and trends evaporate in a click. Yet, how do we create environments that refuse to be forgotten?

Enter Studio Musa. For their latest project, the design studio redefines the retail experience for 545, rejecting the cold, pristine commercialism of traditional storefronts in favor of something far more radical: a lived-in, domestic sanctuary. By weaving together historical weight and modern intimacy—anchored by a monumental travertine portal and a narrative of sequential rooms—they have crafted a space that instructs the body to slow down, breathe, and inhabit rather than consume.

Below, Studio Musa breaks down the philosophy of choreographing memory, the tension of the timeless, and what it means to build a world where the temporary becomes unforgettable.

 

Athena Kuang: Studio Musa operates at the intersection of architecture, fashion, and contemporary culture. Today, these disciplines are highly fast-paced and temporary—pop-ups are built to last a weekend, trends shift in weeks. Yet, architecture requires a sense of permanence. How do you negotiate the tension between the immediate, fast impact of fashion and the slow, lasting resonance of interior architecture?

Studio Musa: We don’t simply design spaces. We build worlds that people can step into. Before thinking about architecture, we always ask ourselves the same question: how should this place make people feel? Once we understand that, everything else begins to fall into place. Materials, light, proportions and objects all become part of the same narrative.

For us, architecture has never been just about creating beautiful environments. It is about shaping the way people move through a space, relate to it and, hopefully, remember it long after they have left.

This is why we don’t see a conflict between the temporary nature of fashion and the slower rhythm of architecture. We’ve all visited places that still exist but can barely remember. At the same time, we’ve experienced temporary spaces that stayed with us for years. Permanence isn’t something we associate with time; we associate it with memory.

Fashion has the ability to capture the present. Architecture has the ability to give that moment a physical form. What interests us is finding the point where those two worlds meet. We don’t design spaces to follow trends, we design places that express an identity. If the concept is honest, the project naturally resists becoming dated.

We often describe our work as designing the temporary to be timeless. Not because we believe temporary architecture should imitate permanence, but because we believe the emotions a place leaves behind always outlast its physical presence.

AK: Retail spaces are usually designed to look pristine and commercial, but you wanted 545 to feel like a real, lived-in home. What are the specific design choices—whether in materials, lighting, or layout—that actually make a space feel “domestic” rather than just another shop?

SM: The ambition was never to recreate a house. It was to imagine what the home of 545 could feel like.

After working closely with the brand for more than a year, we had naturally become immersed in its world. We understood that 545 wasn’t looking for a conventional retail environment. They wanted a place where people could meet, spend time together and recognise themselves in the values of the brand.

A home is probably the only place where we don’t feel like visitors. It’s where conversations happen spontaneously, where music plays in the background, where people stay without feeling the need to justify their presence. We wanted the store to evoke that same sense of ease.

Today, people rarely connect with brands through products alone. They connect through places that make them feel welcome. That’s why our goal wasn’t to create a beautiful display for clothes, but a place where visitors could step inside the universe of 545 before discovering its collection.

Every decision supports this idea. Warm materials such as wood and travertine, soft lighting, books, records, artworks and carefully selected objects all contribute to creating an atmosphere that feels lived in rather than staged.

Even the red carpet carries meaning. As 545 introduced red as a new colour within its identity, we wanted the floor, the very foundation of the space, to embody that new beginning. Visitors encounter it before anything else, almost as the first chapter of a new story for the brand. Ultimately, we wanted people to leave remembering how the place made them feel, not simply what they had seen.

AK: At the physical center of 545 is a travertine portal. Travertine is historically monumental—heavy, mineral, and ancient—yet you’ve used it as a soft symbolic threshold, an invitation to pass into a more intimate realm. Can you talk about the physical and emotional weight of this portal? Why choose a material so deeply rooted in architectural history to mark this contemporary transition?

SM: The portal was never designed to impress people. It was designed to change the way they moved through the space.

In every home there comes a moment when you instinctively understand that you’ve crossed into a more private world. No one tells you; the atmosphere simply changes. We wanted visitors to experience that same feeling inside the store.

Crossing the travertine portal marks the point where the space becomes quieter and more intimate. From there, the store unfolds as a sequence of rooms, each one gradually becoming more private until reaching the fitting rooms, discreetly concealed behind a warm wooden wall.

We chose travertine because it carries an extraordinary architectural memory. It is a material deeply rooted in history, often associated with monumentality, yet it also possesses an unexpected warmth. That contrast fascinated us. It allowed the portal to feel significant without becoming imposing.

Wood completes this transition. After the mineral presence of the stone, it introduces softness, warmth and protection, embracing what we consider the most intimate part of the retail journey.

The portal doesn’t separate two rooms. It marks the moment when visiting a store begins to feel a little more like entering someone’s home.

AK: The layout of the 545 store unfolds as a sequential progression of rooms, gradually shifting from shared spaces to more enclosed, private ones. In a home, we navigate this hierarchy instinctively. How did you choreograph this physical journey for a stranger walking oﬀ the street? How do you gently instruct the body to slow down as it moves deeper into the space?

SM: We wanted the store to reveal itself gradually, never all at once.

Just like in a home, you don’t understand the entire space from the entrance. Every room hints at another, inviting you to continue exploring. That sense of discovery became one of the guiding principles of the project.

Rather than directing visitors through conventional retail strategies, we wanted architecture itself to guide the body. Materiality became part of this choreography.

The travertine portal signals the transition into a quieter and more intimate dimension. The warmth of the wooden wall welcomes visitors into the most private area of the store. The continuous red carpet creates a subtle sense of continuity underfoot while introducing the brand’s new visual identity. Lighting also changes almost imperceptibly throughout the journey, becoming softer as visitors move deeper into the space.

None of these gestures is dramatic on its own, but together they encourage people to slow down naturally. We didn’t want people to walk through the store eﬃciently. We wanted them to pause, browse, sit down, listen to music, have a conversation. In other words, we wanted them to inhabit the space rather than simply consume it. If visitors forget, even for a few minutes, that they’re inside a shop, then we feel we’ve achieved what we set out to do.

AK: Your work has a strong “curatorial eye”—it doesn’t just feel built; it feels collected. How do you choose objects, lighting, and textures that feel like they have a history?

SM: Curating a space begins long before choosing objects.

Our process always starts with observation. Every project has its own character, its own atmosphere and its own rhythm. Before making any design decision, we try to understand what makes that particular project unique and what story it has the potential to tell.

Our shared academic background and our passion for art naturally shape the way we see architecture. References to Bauhaus, Modernism, Postmodernism and Art Deco, together with artists and architects such as Sol LeWitt, Mark Rothko, Gio Ponti, Angelo Mangiarotti and Le Corbusier, are constantly present in our visual memory. They are rarely direct references; they simply become part of the way we think.

We don’t choose objects because they are beautiful. We choose them because of the relationships they create with one another and with the architecture around them.

For us, the most interesting interiors are the ones that feel as though they have evolved over time. They don’t look composed all at once, they feel quietly collected, layer after layer.

Perhaps that’s why we are drawn to spaces that leave a little room for ambiguity. We like it when people can’t immediately tell whether something has always been there or has just been placed there. That uncertainty makes a place feel alive. And when a space feels alive, people naturally begin to make it their own.

items.title: Miles Away: Reactivating the Pulse of an Icon
items.content:
Fashion, at its most potent, is not merely about representation—it is about reactivation. In “MILES AWAY,” a striking two-part photographic story captured by photographer Gabriel Gómez and styled by art director Ayrton Luc-Clément, style becomes a conduit for a legendary, spectral energy. The project is structured as a physical and visual transmission, paying homage to an absent figure while casting his aesthetic rhythm directly into the contemporary arena. Through sharp tailoring, somatic movement, and deliberate spatial design, the editorial manifests as a dialogue between history and the modern body.

The first volume introduces a stark, minimalist environment where the boundary between the human form and the technological system begins to dissolve. Set against neutral walls, models Ekko and Hollow navigate a landscape scattered with analog remnants—tangled audio cables, vinyl records, amplifiers, and even a vintage synthesizer.

The garments worn in this volume serve as the new circuit through which the pressure of the past is felt. Ekko stands in a sharp, three-piece suit and shirt, anchored by elegant shoes. Hollow complements this structured classicism in a sleek, draped look, but is also styled in a textured coat and scarf, leather trousers, polished shoes, and dark shades.

Towards the end of the volume, the imagery takes a surreal turn, featuring models suspended in gravity-defying poses wearing Moncler and Gardouch, and interacting with metallic, fish-shaped balloons while styled in pieces from Carven, Ferragamo, and Vautrait. Rather than attempting to reconstruct historical jazz style, Volume I uses these clothing choices to ground a classic cool in the present. The silhouettes fluctuate between rigid and soft, highlighted by Hollow in a dress paired with a classic shirt and a simple beanie, while Ekko wears fluid, dark separates paired with refined shoes. Towards the end of the volume, the imagery takes a surreal turn, featuring models suspended in gravity-defying poses wearing voluminous technical outerwear, and interacting with metallic, fish-shaped balloons while styled in tailored, sculptural pieces.

Towards the end of the volume, the imagery takes a surreal turn, featuring models suspended in gravity-defying poses wearing voluminous technical outerwear, and interacting with metallic, fish-shaped balloons while styled in tailored, sculptural pieces.

If the first volume established the intellectual and aesthetic circuits of the project, Volume II returns that signal directly to the flesh. The visual landscape shifts dramatically from sterile whites to an intense, absorbing blue, reminiscent of martial arts dojos or sensory deprivation chambers.

 

 

Here, the images behave like a visual cardiac massage—pressing relentlessly against silence and isolation until physical movement returns. The cool blue backdrop is pierced by an intense red jumpsuit paired with minimalist shoes, worn by Hollow, creating a high-contrast visual beat.

Ekko is similarly enveloped in the space wearing draped, tonal garments. The models wrestle, fall, and support each other, mirroring a CPR gesture or an intense dance. The clothing moves with them, whether it is Hollow in a structured coat, jacket, and trousers with refined shoes, or Ekko in a timeless plaid suit and tie contrasted against classic loafers. The narrative concludes not in perfect, sterile harmony, but in a sustained pulse, leaving an exploration of proximity, breath, and the persistent desire for contact.
